analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top tax rate on investment gains from 20 percent to 15 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the top capital gains rate to 15 percent was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on October 4, 2001 and never advanced, receiving no hearing, vote, or further action in the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lower the maximum federal tax rate on long-term capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets held more than a year — from 20 percent to 15 percent. Because most taxable capital gains go to households in the top income brackets, the largest dollar benefit would flow to high earners and investors. The bill was introduced by Rep. Paul Ryan and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who realize long-term capital gains, especially the wealthiest households, who pay the top 20 percent rate on gains; also banks and brokerage firms whose clients' gains are taxed less.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors with large capital gains

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the top capital gains rate from 20 percent to 15 percent, cutting federal tax on long-term investment profits by a quarter at the top rate.
Applies the lower rate to the current tax year upon enactment, including transition rules splitting gains earned before and after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, since reduced tax on gains must be offset by other taxes, borrowing, or spending restraint.

drawbacks.text: Because capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, most of the tax cut would go to the wealthiest taxpayers.
No accompanying revenue source or offset is provided, so the bill would add to federal deficits or require spending cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, targeted tax cut to investors with significant gains but offers little direct benefit to households with little or no capital gains income, and it does not pay for itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on October 4, 2001 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never considered it, so it died without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Paul Ryan on October 4, 2001 and referred to Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Capital gains rates stayed at 20 percent, so no taxpayer group changed position; the bill's single cosponsor and sponsor gained no policy change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — capital gains rates unchanged

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the capital gains rate and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and took no action, letting it die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and only cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrats supported it.

industries.note: Would pay less tax on realized gains, with the benefit concentrated among those with the most investment income.
